html:
The polio vaccine protects against polio, a virus that can paralyse and kill, mostly young children. The first effective one was made by Jonas Salk and announced as safe in April 1955.

In the first half of the 20th century, polio epidemics hit the rich world every summer. President Franklin D. Roosevelt had been paralysed by it, and the charity he founded, the March of Dimes, paid for Salk's work at the University of Pittsburgh.

Salk used a killed virus, given by injection. In 1954 it was tested on more than a million children, one of the largest medical trials ever. Salk did not patent it.

Albert Sabin then made an oral vaccine from a weakened live virus, cheap enough to give on a sugar cube. It was tested on millions in the Soviet Union and came into wide use in the early 1960s.

Since the Global Polio Eradication Initiative began in 1988, cases have fallen by more than 99 percent. Wild polio survives only in Pakistan and Afghanistan. If it is wiped out, it will follow smallpox, the first disease beaten with help from Jenner's vaccine.
